transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-07
Start: 16:00 PT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Rivers (Redwood AE), Samira Khan (Redwood SE), Jin Park (CTO - Montara), Maya Ortiz (SRE Lead), Liam Chen (ML Eng)

Summary: quick hands-on lab to walk through console tracing, error hypothesis building, request log stitching, and a proposed pilot. Focus on how to map inference errors to KV-cache/quantization behaviors and region failover traces.

Topics: console tracing overview; trace <-> request log stitching; identifying error signatures; simulated fallback/trace playback; pilot scoping; security/PII sanitization for logs.

-- Transcript --
[00:00] Alex Rivers: hey everyone, uh thanks for joining. i think we got about 50 minutes, hoped to run a short lab and leave time for q's. can everyone hear okay?
[00:14] Jin Park: yeah, loud and clear. thanks Alex.
[00:18] Samira Khan: awesome. i'll share my screen in a sec, showing the console trace inspector and the request timeline.
[00:28] Maya Ortiz: quick note — we pulled up a couple of failed requests from last week that looked like increased tail latency and a handful of 5xxs.
[00:34] Samira Khan: perfect, that's exactly what i wanted to use. i'm opening the trace map now — you might see some labels that are a little off, the auto transcription of names sometimes messes them up, so ignore that.
[00:52] Speaker 2: (mumble) yeah.
[00:56] Samira Khan: okay jump to a single request, you can see the request path across zones, there's a KV cache hit/miss series inline — note the miss at step 4 correlates with a 180ms token stall.
[01:12] Liam Chen: are those timestamps absolute or relative to the request?
[01:16] Samira Khan: they're relative from request start. the UI shows seq token timing and the kernel selection tag — sometimes the kernel tag is mis-labeled as "kerno" in the transcription, sorry — but it's the runtime kernel choice.
[01:32] Alex Rivers: quick context — Montara runs a batch of short conversational prompts with lots of repetitive prefixes, so prefix caching should help but also creates weird cold miss patterns when you shift model variants.
[01:48] Maya Ortiz: yep, and we saw a spike after a deploy last Thursday, that's when the 5xxs cropped up.
[01:56] [02:00] Samira Khan: okay i'm toggling on the request logs panel — you can stitch logs to traces using the request id or the user session id; we often recommend a primary key of request_id + model_variant for deterministic joins.
[02:18] Jin Park: hmm our current logs only have session and a hashed id, not full request ids — will that break things?
[02:26] Samira Khan: it's okay, you can still stitch using session+timestamp with a small tolerance window, but it's noisy. that's why we asked for a 24h sample of your logs — sanitized — so we can prototype the stitching queries.
[02:44] Liam Chen: would the stitching queries be expensive? we have high log volume.
[02:48] Alex Rivers: they can be, if you try full-text joins. best practice is to emit a short request_id at the application edge and forward it through the inference call. that's light and makes joins trivial.
[03:06] Maya Ortiz: security question — if we send logs, what should we redact? we have PHI in some prompts.
[03:14] Samira Khan: good call — redact any user PII/PHI. we only need request metadata and timing, model variant, token counts, and error codes. if you want, we'll share a sample sanitization script with regex recommendations.
[03:30] Jin Park: please do.
[03:34] [03:39] Samira Khan: switching now to error signature detection — the console has a heatmap for error frequency by upstream kernel, quantization profile, and region. see this spike here labeled "quant-128-m" — that often indicates a quantization mismatch.
[03:56] Alex Rivers: to be explicit, sometimes a quant profile change reduces numeric stability for rare tokens which shows up as garbled output or soft fails that later become 5xx.
[04:12] Liam Chen: wait, can the model itself cause 5xxs? i thought 5xx is infra.
[04:18] Samira Khan: usually infra, but the runtime can throw errors if kv cache pointers get corrupted after a model variant change — that's an example where model+runtime interplay produces infra-like errors.
[04:34] Maya Ortiz: that's interesting. in our case the spike happened after a model package update — could be related.
[04:40] Alex Rivers: exactly. so step one in debugging is hypothesis building — did we change quant profile? did we change kernel selection heuristics? did latency increase at a particular sequence length?
[04:56] [05:00] Samira Khan: i'm now demonstrating trace replay — console can replay a request path against a sandboxed runtime and surface the stage where the error occurs. note this is not live traffic, it's replay against the saved inputs.
[05:18] Jin Park: does the replay account for KV cache warm state?
[05:22] Samira Khan: there's an option to pre-seed the cache with prefix snapshots; if you don't pre-seed you'll see cold-miss behavior, which is useful to reproduce misses that only happen on cold starts.
[05:36] Liam Chen: and the seeded snapshot is just a blob we upload? any size limits?
[05:40] Samira Khan: small limit on UI uploads, but via the API you can stream larger snapshots. we'll include that in the playbook.
[05:50] [06:06] Maya Ortiz: one pain point — we have multi-region failover, and sometimes traces get split across regions in the UI; it's hard to follow the flow.
[06:16] Alex Rivers: we can filter by route and region, but also the console has a cross-region stitching mode — it shows causal edges even if spans hop clouds; sometimes the UI label reads "Vee PC" instead of VPC because of transcription, lol.
[06:34] Jin Park: haha noted.
[06:40] [07:00] Samira Khan: jumping to anomaly detection — console flags unusual token timings with a score. you can link flagged examples to prompt sets so your QA can run targeted manual checks.
[07:14] Liam Chen: can we export flagged examples as a CSV for our SRE workflow?
[07:18] Samira Khan: yes, exportable with metadata and links back to the trace. we'll add a sample export to the repo.
[07:30] [08:02] Alex Rivers: quick sidebar on cost: some customers worry that enabling detailed request tracing increases egress/log costs. we recommend sampling or periodic windows for high-volume endpoints.
[08:18] Maya Ortiz: that's our concern — we need to keep logs for 30 days for compliance, can't push that much data.
[08:26] Alex Rivers: ok, sampling + aggregated histograms is the compromise — you still get signal for regressions without full retention.
[08:38] [09:10] Samira Khan: let's run a short mock postmortem on the sample failing request you provided. i'm going to annotate the timeline: 0-120ms kernel selection, 120-300ms token stall at kv miss, 300-340ms retry, 340ms 5xx surface. hypothesis: cache pointer invalidation after variant switchover.
[09:36] Jin Park: if that's the case, what's the mitigation?
[09:40] Samira Khan: mitigation routes: rollback model variant, apply graceful warmup with prefix preseed, or enable fallback to a quantized-compatible variant. console supports defining a policy for automatic fallback.
[09:56] Liam Chen: how deterministic is the fallback? we can't have silent quality regressions.
[10:02] Alex Rivers: it's policy-driven — you can require either majority model agreement or an eval score threshold; plus we log every fallback occurrence so QA can review.
[10:18] [10:44] Maya Ortiz: ok, let's talk pilot scope. we want a non-prod pilot first, using dedicated capacity for 2 weeks to measure tail lat and cost delta.
[10:54] Samira Khan: recommended: pick 3 representative routes, enable full tracing for 72h to get baseline, then run dedicated pool with identical load for 48h. we provide the dashboard templates and the exact queries.
[11:12] Jin Park: timeline — can we do baseline next week?
[11:18] Alex Rivers: yes — we can deliver the playbook and sample queries by Friday, 2026-04-10. then you provide sanitized logs by 2026-04-13 and we schedule the pilot week of 2026-04-20.
[11:34] [11:58] Liam Chen: elasticity question — if pilot shows improved tail, do we have autoscale config recommendations?
[12:04] Samira Khan: yes, we have autoscale recipes depending on latency percentiles and burst patterns, plus suggested cache sizing. we'll include those in the recommendations doc.
[12:18] Maya Ortiz: favoring safety, we also need SOC2 docs and details about KMS integration for private deployments.
[12:26] Alex Rivers: noted — i'll send SOC2/ISO attestation and the KMS integration guide.
[12:34] [12:58] Jin Park: who should I send the sanitized logs to?
[13:02] Alex Rivers: upload to the secure share link i'll provide in the follow-up email; we'll confirm permissions.
[13:10] Samira Khan: last demo bit — i'll show a quick query that finds requests with kernel-change + token-spike. Query: SELECT request_id, model_variant, token_spike_ms FROM traces WHERE token_spike_ms > 100 AND kernel_changed = true ORDER BY token_spike_ms DESC LIMIT 50; note the field names in your logs may differ.
[13:38] Liam Chen: nice.
[13:42] [14:06] Alex Rivers: ok wrapping up — recap and next steps.
[14:12] Maya Ortiz: quick Q — any known incompatibilities with our KVM based HSM?
[14:18] Alex Rivers: no show-stoppers; our private deployments integrate with customer KMS/HSM; we'll surface specific notes for KVM in the PKI guide.
[14:30] Samira Khan: action items i captured: share playbook + sample queries, sample sanitization script, KV cache recommendation doc.
[14:40] Jin Park: thanks, that was super helpful.
[14:44] Alex Rivers: great. i'll follow up with the links and the pilot calendar invite. thanks everyone.

End of meeting.

Notes: occasional transcription glitches where "kernel" became "kerno", "VPC" read as "Vee PC" or "VPCk"; speaker overlaps in early section. Audio quality medium but all critical points captured.
